results.webTitle: Did you solve it? A new goat for puzzledom’s GOAT

fields.body:
Earlier today I set you a new twist on the Monty Hall problem, which is (according to AI) the most discussed recreational maths puzzle in history.

The standard Monty Hall problem is as follows:

You are a contestant on the US game show Let’s Make a Deal. Monty Hall, the host, asks you to choose one of three doors. Behind one door is a car. Behind the other two are goats. To win the car, which is what you want, you must choose the correct door.

You choose a door. Before your chosen door is opened, however, Monty Hall opens one of the other two doors that he knows has a goat behind it.

He opens the door and it reveals a goat. He now offers you chance to switch your choice to the other door. Do you stick, or do you switch?

The answer is that it makes sense to switch, because you double your odds of winning from 1/3 to 2/3. The puzzle is the subject of debate because the intuitive answer is that switching should not make any difference.

Now to today’s version:

Monty Hall and the golden goat

You are a contestant playing the Monty Hall problem. However, you secretly know one of the goats is the former pet of an eccentric billionaire who lost it and is willing to pay an enormous amount for its return, way more than the car is worth. You really want that goat. The host is unaware of this. After you pick your door, as is traditional, the host opens one door, which he knows doesn’t have the car. He reveals a goat, which you can tell is the ordinary goat and not the secretly valuable one. The host offers to let you switch doors. Should you?

Solution No, you should not!

What is interesting here is that when you want to win the car it makes sense to switch, but when you don’t want to win the car it makes sense to stick!

The easiest way to explain the answer is to look at frequencies. Suppose the game is played a large number of times, say 3,000 times.

The expected number of games in which your initial choice is the (door with the) car is 1,000. Then the expected number of times the host opens the door with the ordinary goat is 500. (Because the host cannot tell between goats, and we assume that the host choses a goat at random.)

The expected number of games in which your initial choice is the (door with the) ordinary goat is 1,000. Then the expected number of times the host opens the door with the ordinary goat is 0.

The expected number of games win which your initial choice is the (door with the) golden goat is 1,000. Then the expected number of times the host opens the door with the ordinary goat is 1000.

So in 3,000 trials, the host will open the door with the ordinary goat 1500 times. If you stick you will win in 1000 trials, a win probability of 2/3, and if you switch you will win in 500 trials, a win probability of 1/3. It is better to stick.

I hope you enjoyed this puzzle. I’ll be back in two weeks.

Credit: The earliest reference seems to be here. Thanks to Henk Tijms for alerting it to me.

I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

results.webTitle: Can you solve it? A new goat for puzzledom’s GOAT

fields.trailText: Take this puzzle by the horns
fields.body:
Today’s puzzle is a new twist on The Monty Hall problem, arguably the greatest maths puzzle of all time.

(According to Gemini, who trawled the internet for me, it is the most discussed and debated recreational maths puzzle of all time.)

Here’s how it goes, for those who may be unaware of it. You are a contestant on the US game show Let’s Make a Deal. Monty Hall, the host, asks you to choose one of three doors. Behind one door is a car. Behind the other two are goats. To win the car, which is what you want, you must choose the correct door.

You choose a door. Before your chosen door is opened, however, Monty Hall opens one of the other two doors that he knows has a goat behind it.

He opens the door and it reveals a goat. He now offers you chance to switch your choice to the other door.

Do you stick, or do you switch?

The intuitive reaction is that it makes no difference. If there are two doors left, surely each door has a 50/50 chance of having the car? This reasoning is fallacious. If you stick with your original choice you have a 1/3 chance of winning the car, but if you switch you double your odds to 2/3. Switch!

Now here’s today’s twist, which has recently been doing the rounds on the net. The set up is the same – but once Monty Hall has opened the door with the goat, you want to win the other goat, not the car.

Monty Hall and the golden goat

You are a contestant playing the Monty Hall problem. However, you secretly know one of the goats is the former pet of an eccentric billionaire who lost it and is willing to pay an enormous amount for its return, way more than the car is worth. You really want that goat. The host is unaware of this. After you pick your door, as is traditional, the host opens one door, which he knows doesn’t have the car. He reveals a goat, which you can tell is the ordinary goat and not the secretly valuable one. The host offers to let you switch doors. Should you?

I’ll be back at 5pm UK with the solution.

PLEASE NO SPOILERS. Please discuss goats, and GOATS.

UPDATE: Read the solution here.

results.webTitle: Starwatch: Vega the bright star will light the way to the constellation of Lyra

fields.trailText: Lyra, the lyre, represents the harp played by the Greek poet Orpheus
fields.body:
We turn our attention this week to one of the sky’s smallest constellations. High overhead from the UK after darkness falls, Lyra, the lyre, is easy to find thanks to the brilliant white star of Vega.

The chart shows the view facing south and looking up towards the zenith from London at 22:30 BST on 17 August.

As the fifth-brightest star in the night sky, Vega forms one corner of the summer triangle, with Deneb in Cygnus, the Swan, and Altair in Aquila, the Eagle, marking the other two.

Having located Vega, the rest of the constellation is easy to trace even though the stars are much fainter. One of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations, Lyra has the distinction of being a star pattern that actually looks like the figure it is named after. It represents the harp played by the Greek poet Orpheus.

In Greek mythology, Orpheus played such beautiful music that he could charm wild animals, move rocks and even influence the gods. Becoming one of the Argonauts, Orpheus’s music protected the rest of the crew from the beguiling call of the Sirens.

Observers in the southern hemisphere can also find Lyra on August evenings, although it remains much lower in the northern sky.

fields.trailText: Professor of anthropology whose approach to archaeology centred on crafts executed by women 40,000 years ago
fields.body:
Olga Soffer, who has died aged 83, brought a revolutionary idea into the conversation about prehistoric ice age people: women mattered. Inspired when working on archaeological excavations in the former USSR, and by remains from a dig in Moravia, in the 1990s she presented a case for women as makers of textiles, baskets and nets, critical to survival in bleak northern conditions 30,000 years ago.

Her achievement was the more remarkable for her career path. By then a professor of anthropology at the University of Illinois, she had obtained her three degrees over three decades, partly while also working as a cosmetics buyer and fashion promoter for a New York department store.

Since the 20s, Soviet Russia, looking to historical materialism, generously funded large archaeological excavations. Unlike most of her colleagues in the west, Soffer, whose family had fled Tito’s Yugoslavia and settled in Brooklyn in 1955, could read the reports. In 1977 she began years of travel and research, supported by grants from the US government, the National Geographic Society and many others. Among 30 sites she worked on, four stood out: Mezhyrich, Ukraine; Avdeevo, Russia; and Dolní Věstonice and Pavlov, Moravia (now in Czechia).

At such places, people built tent-like houses with mammoth bones. At Mezhyrich, 160 kilometres south of Kyiv, male archaeologists credited the remains to heroic male hunters. To Soffer there were too many mammoths – one house was assembled from 95 jaws. She argued instead that the bones had been collected from natural death sites, while noting that archaeologists had overlooked remains of smaller animals. “Maybe they killed one mammoth every 10 years,” she commented, “and never stopped talking about it.”

Already doubting the existence of male-dominated ice age communities, in 1990 she noticed marks in a few tiny clay fragments excavated decades before at Pavlov. She showed them to James Adovasio, an archaeologist at Mercyhurst College, Pennsylvania, who had been digging with her at Mezhyrich, and who knew about basketry and textiles. He recognised impressions of woven threads. They went on to identify 79 such marks among thousands of clay scraps, from Dolní Věstonice and Pavlov, with explosive implications.

Adovasio saw evidence, fortuitously imprinted in clay, for cordage, plaited basketry and woven textiles, made from plants, not animal sinews or hides. Soffer found indications of dress and headgear, previously overlooked in favour of attention to breasts and buttocks (characterised by Soffer as “paleoerotica”), on small female figurines, many of which were found at Avdeevo (carved from mammoth ivory and stone) and Dolní Věstonice (ceramic), similar to the Venuses of Willendorf, west of Vienna, and Kostenki, south of Voronezh, in Russia. Soffer later wrote that the head of the Willendorf figurine offered the clearest depiction of a fibre-based woven cap or hat, “rather than a hairdo, as posited by scholars”.

With Adovasio and his colleague David Hyland, Soffer conjured a world featuring mats, wall hangings, blankets and bags, shawls, shirts, skirts and sashes. Knotted string suggested nets, used by women to hunt small animals. She compared Palaeolithic tailoring to “something from Donna Karan or Calvin Klein”. A figurine’s beaded string item was a “skirt … to die for”. “We’re not talking protection from the elements here,” she told the New York Times.

The sophistication of the weaving and cord-making prompted Adovasio to suggest a history that went back at least 40,000 years. Noting more recent practices, they believed the crafts would have been invented and executed by women.

In 2007 Soffer and Adovasio co-authored, with the science writer Jake Page, The Invisible Sex: Uncovering the True Roles of Women in Prehistory, in which they addressed a perceived male bias. It was widely reported, but the public narrative of ice age life was led by Jean Auel, whose multi-million-selling Earth’s Children novel series was to end in 2011. Soffer was consulted on two titles (The Mammoth Hunters and The Plains of Passage), but the protagonist Ayla, a blond, blue-eyed modern human who challenges the patriarchal world of Neanderthals, nonetheless wears animal skins. Soffer’s wider message, that what survives from the ancient past is a tiny and often misleading representation of reality, has yet to be absorbed, even by many archaeologists.

Olga was born in Nazi-occupied Belgrade. As an infant she was taken with her maternal grandparents to a labour camp: she was treated favourably by the camp commander, she was told, due to her Aryan colouring and looks.

Her parents, Galina (nee Girs) and Alexander Shabunin, came from Russian migrant families scattered after the 1917 Bolshevik revolution. In New York, reached via Yugoslavia and four years in a displaced persons camp in Italy, her father assembled window blinds and her mother worked as a seamstress, while Olga went to Thomas Jefferson high school in Brooklyn.

After obtaining a BA in political science (1965) at Hunter College, City University of New York, she began working at Abraham & Straus, a Brooklyn-based department store chain, first as an assistant buyer for cosmetics, then special events coordinator for fashion. In the latter role she created a gourmet festival featuring the television chef James Beard, and hired a young Brooke Shields as a model.

Bored with work, she took night courses in art history at Hunter, which led to an interest in archaeology and ethnography, and her eventual MA in anthropology there (1975).

In 1978, having gone part-time at the store, she became an adjunct instructor of anthropology at Hunter, moving to Lehman College, then the University of Wisconsin at Milwaukee. After a PhD on the archaeology of eastern Europe at the Graduate Center, City University of New York (1984), Soffer joined the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as assistant professor of anthropology. She rose to professor, with stints as visiting archaeology professor at the Centre de Recherches Archéologiques, France (1992), and heading the department of Slavic languages and literature at Illinois (1993–98). She retired in 2008 as professor emerita. Her awards included an honorary doctorate from the Russian Academy of Sciences.

Both her marriages, to Mark Soffer, a history teacher, in 1962, and Dmitry Bobyshev, a poet and professor of Russian literature, in 1979, ended in divorce. She is survived by her daughter from her first marriage, Alex, and two grandchildren, Jake and Mena.

• Olga Soffer, archaeologist, born 9 September 1942; died 20 June 2026

results.webTitle: Block export of ‘national treasure’ UK fossils, says MP

fields.trailText: Sale of one of UK’s top collections overseas prompts call new rules to help keep items in country
fields.body:
An MP has called on ministers to change export controls so that significant fossils can be classed as national treasures after one of the UK’s best collections, unearthed on Dorset beaches, was sold overseas.

Last week, a Guardian investigation revealed that an unparalleled collection of fossils from the UK’s Jurassic Coast, comprising hundreds of specimens including ichthyosaurs, had been sold to the Natural History Museum in Abu Dhabi for what one source described as an “eight-figure sum”.

The fossils, which belonged to the Dorset-based private collector Chris Moore, were initially offered to the Natural History Museum (NHM) in London and Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales), but neither institution had the funds to buy them.

Senior figures at Lyme Regis Museum have called on ministers to change the way fossil discoveries are recorded and sold. They said they were not informed of the impending sale of Moore’s collection or given the opportunity to acquire it.

A letter from Bridget Houseago, the director of the museum, to Edward Morello, the Liberal Democrat MP for West Dorset, notes that the UK’s cultural goods export controls – intended to give the country an opportunity to retain objects of outstanding national importance – do not cover fossils and other items of natural history because they are not “made”.

This means that “some important and rare fossils can be sold without an export licence,” the letter states.

Lyme Regis Museum was aware of Moore’s collection and considered it among the best private collections from the Lower Lias of Dorset, containing several unique specimens.

Although the museum understood indirectly that Moore might eventually want to sell some or all of the collection, or have it placed on public display, it was unaware that a sale of the collection was under way at the end of 2025.

Dr Jonathan Evans, the chair of trustees at Lyme Regis (Philpot) Museum trust, said: “The museum was not approached either by Chris Moore, by the NHM or National Museum Cardiff [part of Museum Wales] or by any other government entity to check whether we might be interested in acquiring some or all of the collection.”

Related: Britain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beaches

The earlier Guardian investigation revealed that the NHM in London and Amgueddfa Cymru were required to sign non-disclosure agreements. There is no suggestion the sale of the Moore collection to the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi broke any rules. Existing codes of conduct stress the importance of fossil collecting.

The West Dorset fossil collecting code of conduct notes: “On the rapidly eroding West Dorset coast, fossil collecting is essential if specimens, some of which may be of great scientific value, are to be saved from damage or destruction by the sea.”

But as fossil collectors get older, many more private collections are likely to need new homes.

Evans and Houseago want fossils of exceptional scientific or national significance to be covered by the Waverley criteria – three benchmarks used to determine whether an object is classed as a “national treasure”.

As Arts Council England notes, if at least one of the criteria is met, a temporary export bar can be imposed, giving UK museums and other organisations time to raise the money needed to acquire an object.

Houseago and colleagues have also called on the government to strengthen existing legislation to ensure all accredited UK museums are informed when significant collections are proposed for sale and given the opportunity to act.

“In the same way as with treasure trove, painting and other artefacts, an export ban can be put in place and museums are notified,” Houseago said. “Something similar should be done for fossils and there are existing mechanisms that could be used.”

They also want the government to support a national register of important fossil finds “to protect our natural heritage”.

Morello has written to Fiona Twycross, the minister for museums, heritage and gambling, setting out a series of questions, including whether the government will “explore options to delay or suspend the export of this collection to allow accredited UK museums a final opportunity to raise funds and submit an acquisition proposal, thereby giving the collection the best possible chance of remaining in the United Kingdom?”.

The Natural History Museum in Abu Dhabi previously told the Guardian a large majority of the Chris Moore collection was already on public display.

Morello said: “Our natural history is as important as our cultural history and we should take every step possibly to preserve it for the nation. I hope the government will step in to prevent the loss of this important collection,.”

The Department for Culture, Media and Sport declined to comment.

While some may question whether small museums have the financial means to acquire expensive collections such as Moore’s, Evans was confident the money could have been raised. Houseago pointed to crowdfunding, grants and wealthy benefactors as possible sources of funding.

Houseago said it was important to keep such collections on the Jurassic Coast, an area with a long history of extraordinary fossil discoveries. Mary Anning, the pioneering palaeontologist and fossil dealer, was born in Lyme Regis and, among other finds, discovered the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaurus in 1823.

“Fossils like those in Moore’s collection, are an important part of the history and heritage of West Dorset and Lyme Regis,” Houseago said. “These fossils are a shared cultural asset of national and scientific importance, as well as being part of the physical evidence that supports the Unesco world heritage site designation. Here they have meaning and context, and help us tell the story of our history and geology – which is unique and special to this place.”
